keep: Work can outrun credit and still be worth doing — eight of fourteen childhood vaccines say so.
lede: If lives saved were the measure of fame, he would be a household name.
copy: A blunt, hard-driving Montana farm boy, Hilleman nearly didn't go to college. He became the most productive vaccine scientist who ever lived. He developed more than forty vaccines — measles, mumps, rubella, hepatitis A and B, chickenpox, meningitis and pneumonia among them.

Eight of the fourteen vaccines routinely recommended for children today came from his lab. When his own daughter woke with mumps in 1963, he swabbed her throat, cultured the virus and turned it into the vaccine still used. The strain is named “Jeryl Lynn” after her. During the 1957 flu pandemic he recognized the threat early and pushed industry to produce forty million doses, blunting the outbreak in the United States.
He worked in deliberate obscurity, indifferent to credit. That is precisely why so few people know the name of the man who may have prevented more deaths than anyone in history.

bio.t: Vaccinated: One Man's Quest to Defeat the World's Deadliest Diseases
bio.why: Offit, himself a vaccine inventor, interviewed Hilleman extensively in his final months. Both a biography of an irascible genius and a clear-eyed history of how vaccines are made.

contested: Offit is a colleague and a public vaccine advocate, and the book is admiring by design — there is no critical distance here. The frequently quoted 'eight million lives a year' figure is an estimate with a wide range, not a measured quantity.
